name: Calf & Compression Locks
keyCorrections: If the opponent pulls their leg free, your trap was too shallow — re-enter deeper in your joint crease.
If you cannot get the tap, your shin angle is wrong — rotate your shin so the bone edge presses into their calf.
If they spin out, you lost upper body control — establish a grip on their collar, arm, or far hip.
If your leg gets tired holding the trap, you are using muscle instead of structure — relax and rely on bone contact.
description: Use compression locks (calf slicers) from leg entanglements and guard positions to attack the knee and calf — forcing taps or opening sweeps and back takes.
shortInstruction: Trap the leg, drive your shin bone into their calf, compress — the calf slicer is a three-second submission if the angle is right.
summary: Calf compression locks (slicers) use your shin bone against the opponent's calf muscle with their leg trapped in your joint crease. The compression creates intense pressure on the calf and knee — opponents must tap, expose their back, or give up a sweep. Unlike heel hooks which target rotational knee ligaments, compression locks attack the knee in a different plane and are often available when the heel hook is defended. They work from saddle, 50/50, backside 50/50, half guard, and truck positions. The key to effective compression locks is bone-on-muscle contact with proper shin angle and hip drive.
whyItWorks: The shin bone (tibia) pressing into the calf muscle creates concentrated pressure that few opponents can tolerate.
Compression locks attack the knee in a plane that heel hook defenses do not protect — making them an excellent secondary attack.
They create a dilemma: tap from the calf slicer or give up the sweep/back take.
The mechanics are simple and repeatable — trap, align, compress — making them reliable under pressure.
Calf slicers can be finished with relatively low force when the angle is correct.
commonMistakes: Using the flat of the shin instead of the bone edge — the bone edge creates concentrated pressure.
Leaving space between their leg and your body — the trap must be tight against your chest or hip.
Forgetting to control the opponent's upper body — they will spin out of the compression.
Applying the compression too slowly or tentatively — decisive shin-to-calf contact is more effective.
Over-committing to the finish when the opponent rolls — follow their roll for the sweep or back take.
coachingCues: Bone edge to the calf, flat shin won't cut it.
Trap deep in the joint crease — calf slicers need proximity.
Control the upper body before you squeeze.
If they roll, follow — the sweep is worth more than the tap.
Compression is about angle, not strength.
safetySummary: Calf slicers apply intense pressure to the knee joint and calf muscle — apply slowly and release on tap.
Do not apply compression locks explosively — knee injuries can happen before the opponent feels pain.
Compression locks are not recommended for beginners — proper control and awareness are essential.
Be aware that some partners may have pre-existing knee conditions — establish communication before training.

systemLogic.corePrinciple: Leg entanglement or guard position → trap opponent's leg in your joint crease (knee pit or hip crease) → align shin bone edge against their calf → compress by closing the space → finish or follow the roll.

decisionTree.action: Thread your outside leg over their trapped leg, trap the foot at your hip, drive shin into calf.
Trap their near leg in your knee pit, underhook their far leg, drive shin into calf (bear trap entry).
Leg triangle around their waist, thread shin behind their knee, trap their foot and compress.
Release compression, follow their hips to sweep to top position or take the back.

moneyDetails: The bone edge of your shin (tibia) is the weapon — rotate your shin so the sharp edge, not the flat surface, contacts their calf.
The closer their trapped leg is to your hip or chest, the stronger the compression — proximity creates pressure.
Upper body control (collar tie, underhook, or far wrist) prevents them from spinning out of the compression.
A common entry from saddle: bring your outside leg over their trapped leg, trap their foot at your hip crease, then drive your hips forward to create compression.
From half guard: when they drive forward, trap their near leg in your knee pit, secure an underhook, and roll your hips toward them to create the calf slicer.
nextStep: After calf compression locks, learn the toe hold / Estima lock as another foot attack from leg entanglements.
fixItFast: Leg keeps slipping? Trap it deeper — closer to your hip or chest.
Compression not working? Adjust shin angle — use the bone edge, not the flat.
They roll away? Release the trap, follow their hips, take the back or sweep.
Pain in your own shin? You are using the flat of the shin — rotate to the bone edge.
